title: Liquid-liquid phase separation and a phage-encoded inhibitor cooperatively drive transcriptional transition during phage SPO1 infection.
data_url: https://www.rcsb.org/structure/8XA7 (plus PDB 22DL, BMRB 36822, EMDB-38195/38196); supplement via Europe PMC

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and unzipped the full 40 MB supplement: it contains 3 movies, one figure PDF, a slide deck and one Word file 'Table S1-7.docx'. I parsed that Word file directly and listed every table: S1 strains/plasmids (35 rows), S2 primers (55 rows), S3 NMR refinement statistics (28 rows), S4 three promoter sequences (9 rows), S5 cryo-EM statistics (22 rows); S6 and S7 are embedded screenshots, and I opened the S7 image and read it (10 phage proteins with a 'LLPS (predicted)' score column). I also confirmed the deposited structure 8XA7 downloads from RCSB (HTTP 200) and EMD-38195 metadata returns from EMDB.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: All biology: that Gp27 drives condensate formation in vitro and in vivo, that Gp33 traps RNA polymerase in an inactive state, and the microscopy/transcription-assay results. Those measurements exist only as figures and movies, not as any numeric table in the supplement.

a1_downloadable.note: Open access with no login. I confirmed PDB 8XA7 coordinates download (HTTP 200) and EMDB EMD-38195 metadata returns; the 40 MB supplement unzipped fine.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL, checked in the files, not just the paper. Nothing in the supplement is a prediction target. The paper's actual measurements (does a protein form droplets, how much transcription each promoter gives) appear only as microscopy images, gel panels and movies; any label would have to be constructed by reading values off figures.

a3_inputs_present.note: Protein and promoter sequences are obtainable (SPO1 genome, Table S4 promoters), so inputs would exist even though labels do not.

a4_units_stated.note: Structural statistics tables (S3, S5) state units properly; irrelevant since there is no measurement table to model.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL, counted in the files. The largest biology-relevant table is Table S7 with 10 phage proteins. Everything else is reagents (35 strains, 55 primers) or refinement statistics. The experimental unit here is essentially 2-3 proteins and 3 promoters, against a checklist floor of ~400-1,500 labelled rows.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~41 MB supplement plus a few structure files
a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially laptop-sized; size was never the problem.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Table S6 says eight SPO1 transcription genes and Table S7 lists 10 proteins; both match the text. No count conflict, just tiny counts.

a8_label_provenance.note: FAIL. The only numeric label-like column anywhere is Table S7's 'LLPS (predicted)' score, which is the output of an existing phase-separation predictor applied to 10 phage proteins. Training on that would be distilling another model, which is exactly the circularity A8 forbids.

existing_models.name: PSPire, a machine-learning predictor of phase-separating proteins
existing_models.score_and_split: Published 2024 in Nature Communications; benchmarks report best AUROC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) around 0.84 for proteins with disordered regions and about 0.68 for those without, on curated positive/negative protein sets.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Predicting phase separation for proteins that lack intrinsically disordered regions remains poor (area under the precision-recall curve near 0.08).

existing_models.name: PhaSePred, a multi-feature phase-separation predictor with a public web server
existing_models.score_and_split: Included in several independent benchmarks of 9-19 predictors; evaluated on curated human-dominated positive/negative sets rather than on held-out taxonomic groups.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Coverage of non-human and non-eukaryotic proteins, and separating true condensate formers from merely disordered proteins.

existing_models.name: PSTP and SSPSPredictor, protein-language-model-based phase-separation predictors (2025-2026)
existing_models.score_and_split: Report state-of-the-art residue-level and protein-level phase-separation prediction using ESM-2 (a protein language model) embeddings; splits are curated-database holdouts.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Condition dependence (salt, crowding, partner molecules) and generalisation outside curated databases.

backbone.name: ESM-2 (a protein language model) would be the natural backbone for any phage phase-separation task
backbone.hardware: CPU is sufficient for a few hundred short phage proteins, but there is nothing here to train a head on
backbone.licence: ESM-2 is MIT-licensed; the paper's structures are public-domain PDB/EMDB depositions

integration.partner_dataset: PhaSepDB / DrLLPS / LLPSDB (curated phase-separation protein databases) joinable on UniProt accession
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Do phase-separation predictors trained almost entirely on eukaryotic proteins transfer to phage and bacterial proteins? — a real question, but this paper contributes at most 2 labelled proteins toward answering it.

controls.positive_control: Not applicable: with 2-3 measured proteins there is no train/test structure in which a control could be run.
controls.negative_control: Not applicable for the same reason.
controls.external_validation: PhaSepDB and DrLLPS exist as external sets, but this paper supplies no labelled rows to validate against them.

honest_claim_h3: No honest model-based claim can be made from this paper's data: it reports structures and microscopy for a handful of phage proteins, so any 'model' would be fitted to fewer than ten examples, two of which carry labels copied from an existing predictor.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use phage protein sequence to predict whether the protein forms liquid droplets inside an infected bacterial cell.
plain_idea.train_on: The project I considered would train on phage protein sequences labelled as droplet-forming or not. This paper supplies roughly 2 experimentally characterised proteins (Gp27 forms condensates, Gp33 does not) plus a 10-row table of computationally predicted scores.
plain_idea.predict: A yes/no or probability for condensate formation. The true answer here comes from fluorescence microscopy of tagged proteins in cells and turbidity/droplet assays in vitro, reported only as images in the figures.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Phage biologists and synthetic-biology groups would like to know which phage proteins organise the infection into compartments; but the measurements needed to learn that mapping are not in this paper.

more_or_better_data.why: This paper adds about 2 experimentally characterised phage proteins, against curated databases such as PhaSepDB and DrLLPS that hold thousands of annotated phase-separating proteins used to train PSPire and PhaSePred.

confidence_score.why: No replicate numeric measurements are tabulated anywhere in the supplement, so there is no basis for estimating per-prediction uncertainty.

models_beatable.why: PSPire (2024) and the 2025-2026 protein-language-model predictors PSTP and SSPSPredictor are recent, open and already benchmarked by independent groups across 9-19 tools, including taxonomy-aware splits.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails the first condition outright: there is no training table here to add to a baseline, and the only numeric column available is itself a predictor's output.

ml_idea: The only conceivable task — predict phage protein phase-separation propensity from sequence — cannot be built from this paper. Its labels would have to come from PhaSepDB/DrLLPS, in which case this paper contributes nothing but a two-protein anecdote, and its one numeric column is another model's prediction.

effort.compute_note: Sizes measured from the downloaded 41 MB supplement and structure files; no model training is possible so training-time estimates are null.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the rows in the supplementary tables: the largest biology table has 10 proteins and its only numeric column is labelled '(predicted)'. That took one Word-file parse and killed it.

verdict_reason: Structural and cell-biology paper with no labelled dataset: largest table is 10 proteins whose only numeric column is another predictor's output (A2, A5, A8 all fail).
